extracted.intended_audience: advanced_undergraduate or beginning_graduate students in real analysis / multivariable calculus
extracted.subtask_description: Excerpt from a real-analysis / advanced calculus textbook covering vector-valued extensions (chain rule, Taylor), matrix exponential, partitions of unity, inverse/implicit function theorems, and Riemann integration in several variables; contains precise statements, lemmas, propositions, and proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chain rule extension for compositions
rubrics_metrics.description: The chain rule extends to compositions provided domains are subsets of R^l and the inner function f has values in R^m (while the outer function g may have values in C^k); in compositions g∘f we insist that f have values in R^m.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When extending single-variable proofs to vector-valued contexts, prefer identifying vector ranges and working componentwise (as in Theorem 3.10). The requirement that f take values in R^m (not an arbitrary C^k-range) is emphasized to ensure the chain rule applies cleanly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vector-valued Taylor's theorem prerequisites
rubrics_metrics.description: A vector-valued version of Taylor's Theorem is valid if definitions are adapted so that the Taylor formula remains true component by component; specifically enlarge the definitions of partial derivatives of any order and of 1-dimensional Riemann integration to operate on vector-valued functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no difficulty in extending definitions: treat partial derivatives and integrals componentwise. Ensure the extended definitions agree with componentwise operations so the scalar Taylor results apply to each component.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vector-valued partial derivative / Jacobian identification
rubrics_metrics.description: For f : E → R^m, the vector-valued partial derivative ∂f/∂x_j is defined without passing to components; the entries of this vector-valued partial derivative are exactly the entries of the jth column of the Jacobian matrix of f. Thus the Jacobian matrix consists of the vector-valued partial derivatives of f lined up as columns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reasoning about higher-order partials and Jacobians for vector-valued maps, treat column vectors as partial derivatives and assemble them into the Jacobian; this keeps componentwise manipulations systematic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inequality for Riemann integral of vector-valued functions
rubrics_metrics.description: For a vector-valued integrand F(t) with values in R^m or C^m, the expected inequality holds: ||∫_a^b F(t) dt|| ≤ ∫_a^b ||F(t)|| dt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses the usual inner product on the range (dot product or Hermitian inner product) and the Schwarz inequality. If ∫_a^b F(t) dt = 0 vector the inequality is trivial; otherwise specialize the computation by pairing with unit vectors to derive the scalar inequality and apply Schwarz.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and basic convergence of matrix exponential (Proposition 3.12)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any n-by-n complex matrix A define exp(A) = e^A = sum_{N=0}^∞ A^N / N!. The series converges entry by entry, and every partial derivative of an entry is uniformly convergent on any bounded subset of matrix space; hence exp is C^∞ as a matrix-valued function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use operator-norm estimates to bound ||A^N||/N! and show uniform Cauchy convergence on bounded sets. One may pass from operator norm to Hilbert–Schmidt norm and then argue entrywise uniform convergence. Term-by-term differentiation is justified by uniform convergence of the differentiated series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Properties of the matrix exponential (Proposition 3.13)
rubrics_metrics.description: Key identities: (a) e^X e^Y = e^{X+Y} when X and Y commute; (b) e^X is nonsingular (e^0 = I and e^X has inverse e^{-X}); (c) d/dt e^{tX} = X e^{tX}; (d) similarity conjugation: if W is nonsingular then e^{W^{-1} X W} = W^{-1} e^X W; (e) det(e^X) = e^{Tr X}, where Tr X is the trace of X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proofs rely on series manipulations justified by convergence estimates. For (a) expand both exponentials and reorganize sums using commutativity; for (d) use (W^{-1} X W)^N = W^{-1} X^N W to move W outside the series; for (e) reduce to a one-variable determinant function f(t)=det(e^{tX}) and show f'(t) = (Tr X) f(t), then identify the constant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of partition of unity subordinate to finite open cover (Proposition 3.14)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let K be a compact subset of R^n and {U_1,...,U_k} a finite open cover of K. Then there exist continuous functions φ_1,...,φ_k on R^n with values in [0,1] such that (a) each φ_i is 0 outside some compact set contained in U_i, and (b) sum_{i=1}^k φ_i is identically 1 on K (i.e., {φ_i} is a partition of unity subordinate to the cover).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction uses Lemma 3.15 to shrink opens to those with compact closure contained in the U_i, then builds bump-like continuous functions g_i supported in these shrunk sets, forms a positive sum g = Σ g_i, and normalizes φ_i = g_i / g (adjusted to be 0 where g=0). Remarks note the general metric-space notion and that smooth partitions (C^∞) are available in other treatments when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma on shrinking open covers to compactly supported subcovers (Lemma 3.15)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) If L is compact and U open with L ⊆ U, then there exists an open set V with L ⊆ V and cl(V) compact and cl(V) ⊆ U. (b) If K is compact and {U_1,...,U_n} is a finite open cover of K, then there exists an open cover {V_1,...,V_n} of K with cl(V_i) compact and cl(V_i) ⊆ U_i for each i.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs use the distance function D(x,U^c) which is positive on compact L, choose a radius to get a closed ball inside U, then proceed inductively over the finite cover. This lemma is a standard tool in constructing partitions of unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit Function Theorem (Theorem 3.16)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose F is C^1 from an open set E ⊆ R^{n+m} into R^m and F(a,b)=0 for (a,b)∈E. If the m-by-m matrix [∂F_i/∂y_j](a,b) is invertible, then there exist neighborhoods W of a and U of (a,b) with a unique C^1 function f: W → R^m such that F(x,f(x)) = 0 for x∈W, f(a)=b, and the Jacobian of f is [f'(x)] = - [∂F/∂y]^{-1} [∂F/∂x] evaluated at (x,f(x)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The theorem can be derived from the Inverse Function Theorem by defining φ(x,y)=(x,F(x,y)) and applying local invertibility. The text emphasizes two computational viewpoints (implicit differentiation via total differentials; chain-rule approach) which give the same formulas for derivatives when the implicit solution exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inverse Function Theorem (Theorem 3.17)
rubrics_metrics.description: If φ is C^1 on an open E⊆R^n and φ'(a) is invertible at a∈E, put b=φ(a). Then there exist neighborhoods U of a and V of b such that φ is one-to-one from U onto V, U is of class C^1, the inverse f:V→U is C^1, and f'(φ(x)) = [φ'(x)]^{-1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remarks: The Implicit Function Theorem and Inverse Function Theorem are equivalent; one may derive one from the other. The proof outline: show local injectivity (via derivative estimates), show local onto using compactness of balls (or completeness), then prove continuity and differentiability of the inverse and apply the chain rule to get the derivative formula. If φ is C^k (k≥1) or smooth, so is its inverse on the neighborhood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lower-norm bound for invertible linear maps (Lemma 3.18)
rubrics_metrics.description: If L: R^n → R^n is an invertible linear map, then there exists m>0 such that ||L(y)|| ≥ m ||y|| for all y∈R^n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses existence of linear inverse L^{-1} and bounds ||y|| = ||L(L^{-1} y)|| ≤ ||L|| ||L^{-1}|| ||y||, rearranged to obtain m = 1/||L^{-1}||. This lemma is used to get local Lipschitz-type estimates in proofs of local invertibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local injectivity and estimate using derivative continuity (Lemma 3.19)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given ϕ and invertible linear map ϕ'(a) with lower bound m, there exists δ>0 such that for x,x_0 in B(a,δ) the derivative ϕ'(x) remains invertible and one has estimates showing ϕ is one-to-one on B(a,δ); specifically an inequality of the form ||ϕ(x)-ϕ(x_0)|| ≥ (m/2) ||x-x_0|| holds (quantitative estimate in text).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof applies the Mean Value Theorem componentwise and continuity of ϕ' to control differences ϕ'(x)-ϕ'(a). The lemma yields both injectivity and invertibility of linearizations near a point and provides constants used later to show continuity of inverse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Image of small ball is open (Lemma 3.20)
rubrics_metrics.description: With notation as in Lemma 3.19, ϕ(B(a,δ)) is open in R^n: the image of a sufficiently small ball around a under ϕ is an open neighborhood of ϕ(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proof finds a minimizing point in a closed smaller ball and uses first-derivative conditions: if a minimum of ||ϕ(x)-y|| occurs in the interior, derivatives force a contradiction unless the minimum is zero, ensuring surjectivity onto a small ball around ϕ(a). This lemma helps establish that ϕ is locally onto a neighborhood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smooth inverse/diffeomorphism corollary (Corollary 3.21)
rubrics_metrics.description: If φ is C^k (k≥1) on an open set E and φ'(a) is invertible, then the local inverse f produced by the Inverse Function Theorem is C^k on its domain; in particular if φ is smooth then φ is a diffeomorphism onto its local image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason: the inverse derivative formula expresses derivatives of f as quotients/polynomials in derivatives of φ and the nonvanishing determinant; inductive differentiation shows higher regularity transfers to the inverse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions for Riemann integral in several variables
rubrics_metrics.description: For a bounded function f:A→R on a closed rectangle A = [a_1,b_1]×...×[a_n,b_n], define n-variable partitions P=(P_1,...,P_n) and component rectangles R=[c_1,d_1]×...×[c_n,d_n]. Define mesh μ(P) as maximum side length among component intervals. For each component rectangle R set M_R(f)=sup_{x∈R} f(x), m_R(f)=inf_{x∈R} f(x). Define upper sum U(P,f)=Σ_R M_R(f) |R| and lower sum L(P,f)=Σ_R m_R(f) |R|. The upper Riemann integral is inf_P U(P,f) and the lower is sup_P L(P,f); f is Riemann integrable if these two coincide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These definitions generalize the one-variable theory: build partitions as products of one-dimensional partitions, compute sup/inf on each cell, and take sums weighted by cell volume. Mesh control and refinements play the same role as in one variable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bounds for integrals under boundedness (Lemma 3.22)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f:A→R satisfies m ≤ f(x) ≤ M on A, then for any partition P, m|A| ≤ L(P,f) ≤ U(P,f) ≤ M|A| and consequently m|A| ≤ lower_integral ≤ upper_integral ≤ M|A|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the straightforward extension of the one-variable bounding argument: integrals (upper/lower) lie between bounds times volume. Use for basic estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refinement monotonicity and integrability criterion (Lemma 3.23)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) If P* refines P then L(P,f) ≤ L(P*,f) and U(P*,f) ≤ U(P,f). (b) For any partitions P1,P2, L(P1,f) ≤ U(P2,f). (c) The lower integral ≤ upper integral. (d) If f is continuous on A then f is Riemann integrable. (e) f is integrable iff for each ε>0 there exists a partition P with U(P,f)-L(P,f)<ε.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key tool: uniform continuity of continuous functions on compact rectangles (Heine–Borel) yields integrability. The characterization via arbitrarily small upper-lower gap is the standard Riemann integrability test extended to several variables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity implies Riemann integrability (Theorem 3.24)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is continuous on a closed rectangle A, then f is Riemann integrable on A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use uniform continuity on compact A to choose partitions making oscillation on each cell small and therefore U(P,f)-L(P,f) small; apply Lemma 3.23(e).

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebra and inequalities for multiple integrals (Proposition 3.25)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f1 and f2 are Riemann integrable on A then: (a) f1+f2 is integrable and ∫(f1+f2)=∫f1+∫f2; (b) c f1 integrable and ∫ c f1 = c ∫ f1; (c) if f1 ≤ f2 then ∫ f1 ≤ ∫ f2; (d) if |f1| ≤ M then ∫ |f1| finite and |∫ f1| ≤ ∫ |f1|; (e) f1 f2 and f1^2 are integrable if f1,f2 integrable (statements about products); (f) if f takes values in [m,M] and φ:[m,M]→R is continuous then φ∘f is integrable; (g) p(f1) integrable for polynomial p when f1 integrable (various closure properties).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the standard algebraic closure properties of the Riemann integral extended to several variables; proofs mimic the one-variable arguments using partitions and bounds. Part (f) uses continuity of φ and uniform continuity on [m,M] to pass integrability through composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform-limit preservation of integrability (Theorem 3.26)
rubrics_metrics.description: If {f_n} is a sequence of Riemann integrable functions on A converging uniformly to f on A, then f is Riemann integrable and lim_{n→∞} ∫_A f_n = ∫_A f.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uniform convergence controls oscillation uniformly across partitions, allowing integrability to pass to the limit and interchange of limit and integral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Riemann sums convergence criterion (Theorem 3.27)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is Riemann integrable on A then for any choice of tags t_R in each component rectangle R of a partition P, the Riemann sums S(P,{t_R},f) converge to ∫_A f as the mesh μ(P)→0. Conversely, if f is bounded and there exists r such that for every ε>0 there is δ>0 with |S(P,{t_R},f)-r| < ε whenever μ(P)<δ, then f is Riemann integrable and ∫_A f = r.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct part is more subtle in several variables (proof included in text); the converse parallels the one-variable proof. This gives a practical test: control over all Riemann sums for sufficiently fine meshes characterizes integrability and the integral value.
